records.source: הֲיָדַ֗עְתָּ עֵ֭ת לֶ֣דֶת יַעֲלֵי־סָ֑לַע חֹלֵ֖ל אַיָּל֣וֹת תִּשְׁמֹֽר׃
records.gloss: ? Do you know [the] time of giving birth of [the] goats of [the] rock; [the] calving of [the] does do you watch?
pieces: Do you know when the mountain goats give birth among the rocks? \q Do you watch over the does as they bear their young?

L.1: Do you know the time when the goats of the rock give birth? \q Do you watch the does in labor?

R.1: Do you know when the mountain goats have their young? \q Have you watched the deer give birth?

decisions.choice: God's questions go on from chapter 38
decisions.reason: The speech that began in 38:1 continues without a break. After the lion and the raven (38:39-41), God turns to wild animals that live far from people and asks Job what he knows of their lives, starting with the birth of their young.

decisions.choice: goats of the rock: the wild mountain goat (ibex)
decisions.reason: These goats live on high cliffs where people cannot follow (Psalm 104:18; 1 Samuel 24:3). No one sees when they give birth.

decisions.choice: the calving of the does: deer in the pains of birth
decisions.reason: The verb means to writhe in labor. The does are female deer, whose calving is also an act of God in Psalm 29:9.

decisions.choice: watch: observe closely, keep watch over
decisions.reason: The verb (shamar) means to watch or guard. God asks whether Job has watched over these births, as God himself has.

decisions.choice: mountain goats ... among the rocks (B); mountain goats (R)
decisions.reason: "Goats of the rock" is the Hebrew name for the animal; Balanced gives the usual English name and keeps the rocks as their home, Readable gives only the name.

records.heading: Do you know when the mountain goats give birth?

records.source: תִּסְפֹּ֣ר יְרָחִ֣ים תְּמַלֶּ֑אנָה וְ֝יָדַ֗עְתָּ עֵ֣ת לִדְתָּֽנָה׃
records.gloss: Do you count [the] months [that] they fulfill, and do you know [the] time of their giving birth?
pieces: Can you count the months until they are due, \q and do you know the time when they give birth?

L.2: Do you count the months they fulfill, \q and do you know the time of their giving birth?

R.2: Can you count the months they carry their young? \q Do you know when they will give birth?

decisions.choice: the months they fulfill: the full length of their pregnancy
decisions.reason: To "fulfill" months is to complete the time of carrying young until birth (compare Genesis 25:24, where "her days were fulfilled" to give birth).

decisions.choice: a question of ability: can you count?
decisions.reason: The Hebrew form asks both whether Job does count the months and whether he could. The point is that God knows and keeps these times, and Job does not.

decisions.choice: Can you count
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the sense of ability in the question (m2); Literal keeps the plain "Do you count".

records.source: תִּ֭כְרַעְנָה יַלְדֵיהֶ֣ן תְּפַלַּ֑חְנָה חֶבְלֵיהֶ֥ם תְּשַׁלַּֽחְנָה׃
records.gloss: They kneel down, their young they split open, their labor pains they send forth.
pieces: They crouch down and bring their young to birth; \q they are rid of their labor pains.

L.3: They kneel down, they split open [to bear] their young; \q they send forth their labor pains.

R.3: They kneel down, and their young are born. \q Then their birth pains are over.

decisions.choice: split open: give birth, the young breaking out
decisions.reason: The verb means to cut or split open. It pictures the young breaking out of the womb, a vivid way to say the mother gives birth.

decisions.choice: send forth their labor pains: are done with the pains of birth
decisions.reason: The word means pains, especially the pains of labor (Isaiah 13:8). To send them forth is to be rid of them once the young are born. Because the word can stand for what the pains bring, some take it as "their offspring"; the meaning of the verse is the same.

decisions.choice: bring their young to birth; are rid of (B); are born, are over (R)
decisions.reason: The two Hebrew pictures are kept in Literal. Balanced and Readable say plainly what they mean (m1, m2).

records.source: יַחְלְמ֣וּ בְ֭נֵיהֶם יִרְבּ֣וּ בַבָּ֑ר יָ֝צְא֗וּ וְלֹא־שָׁ֥בוּ לָֽמוֹ׃
records.gloss: Their young grow strong, they grow up in the open; they go out and do not return to them.
pieces: Their young grow strong and grow up in the open country; \q they go off and do not come back to them.

L.4: Their young grow strong, they grow up in the open; \q they go out and do not return to them.

R.4: Their young grow strong in the open fields. \q Then they leave their mothers and never come back.

decisions.choice: in the open: in open country, the wild
decisions.reason: The word (bar) here means the open field, as the same word does in Aramaic (Daniel 4:12). Elsewhere a word spelled the same means grain, which does not fit here.

decisions.choice: to them: to their mothers
decisions.reason: "Them" refers back to the mothers of verses 1-3. The young need no human help; they grow up and leave on their own, and God cares for them.

decisions.choice: leave their mothers
decisions.reason: Readable names the mothers so that "them" is clear (m2).

records.source: מִֽי־שִׁלַּ֣ח פֶּ֣רֶא חָפְשִׁ֑י וּמֹסְר֥וֹת עָ֝ר֗וֹד מִ֣י פִתֵּֽחַ׃
records.gloss: Who sent out [the] wild donkey free, and [the] bonds of [the] wild ass who loosened?
pieces: Who let the wild donkey go free? \q Who untied the ropes of the wild ass?

L.5: Who sent out the wild donkey free? \q And the bonds of the wild ass, who loosened [them]?

R.5: Who set the wild donkey free? \q Who untied its ropes and let it run loose?

decisions.choice: wild donkey, wild ass: two names for the same wild animal
decisions.reason: Both words name the wild donkey of the desert, the onager, as the two lines of the verse say the same thing twice. The second word occurs only here in the Bible. The wild donkey stands for a life no one can tame (6:5; 11:12; 24:5; Genesis 16:12).

decisions.choice: loosened its bonds: made it free
decisions.reason: The wild donkey has never worn a rope. The question pictures God as the one who untied it: he made it to be free.

decisions.choice: its ropes (R)
alternatives: the bonds of the wild ass
decisions.reason: Readable does not repeat a second name for the same animal (m1), and says "its ropes".

records.source: אֲשֶׁר־שַׂ֣מְתִּי עֲרָבָ֣ה בֵית֑וֹ וּֽמִשְׁכְּנוֹתָ֥יו מְלֵֽחָה׃
records.gloss: Which I made [the] desert plain its home, and its dwellings [the] salt land.
pieces: I made the wilderness its home \q and the salt flats its dwelling place.

L.6: [It is the one] whose home I made the desert plain, \q and its dwelling places the salt land.

R.6: I gave it the desert to live in, \q the salty land as its home.

decisions.choice: which: the wild donkey of verse 5
decisions.reason: The verse continues the question of verse 5. God himself ("I") gave the wild donkey its home.

decisions.choice: desert plain, salt land: dry, barren country
decisions.reason: The desert plain ('aravah) is the dry steppe; the salt land is ground where almost nothing grows (Jeremiah 17:6; Psalm 107:34). No one farms there, so no one owns the animal that lives there.

decisions.choice: [It is the one] whose
decisions.reason: Literal supplies a few words so that "which" can follow the question of verse 5; Balanced and Readable start a new sentence.

records.source: יִ֭שְׂחַק לַהֲמ֣וֹן קִרְיָ֑ה תְּשֻׁא֥וֹת נ֝וֹגֵ֗שׂ לֹ֣א יִשְׁמָֽע׃
records.gloss: It laughs at [the] tumult of [the] town; [the] shouts of a driver it does not hear.
pieces: It scorns the noise of the city; \q it never hears the shouts of a driver.

L.7: It laughs at the uproar of the town; \q it does not hear the shouts of a driver.

R.7: It laughs at the noise of the town. \q No driver ever shouts orders at it.

decisions.choice: laughs at: looks down on, scorns
decisions.reason: To laugh at something here is to scorn it as no threat (as 39:18, 22; 41:21). The wild donkey wants nothing of town life.

decisions.choice: a driver: one who drives working animals
decisions.reason: The word (noges) is used for slave drivers in Egypt (Exodus 3:7) and for anyone who drives animals at work. The tame donkey hears his shouts all day; the wild donkey never does.

decisions.choice: No driver ever shouts orders at it
alternatives: it does not hear the shouts of a driver
decisions.reason: Readable says what the line means: the wild donkey never works under a driver (m2).

records.source: יְת֣וּר הָרִ֣ים מִרְעֵ֑הוּ וְאַחַ֖ר כָּל־יָר֣וֹק יִדְרֽוֹשׁ׃
records.gloss: It explores [the] mountains [as] its pasture, and after every green thing it searches.
pieces: It roams the mountains for its pasture \q and searches for every green plant.

L.8: It explores the mountains [as] its pasture, \q and it searches after every green thing.

R.8: It roams the hills to find its food \q and looks for anything green to eat.

decisions.choice: explores: ranges over, searches out
alternatives: what it finds on the mountains
decisions.reason: The verb is used for the spies who went through the land (Numbers 13:2). The wild donkey ranges over the mountains for its food. Some read the word as a noun, "what it finds"; the picture is the same.

decisions.choice: every green thing: whatever grows in dry country
decisions.reason: In the desert and on bare hills little is green. The wild donkey is free, but must search widely; no one brings it food.

records.source: הֲיֹ֣אבֶה רֵּ֣יםעָבְדֶ֑ךָ אִם־יָ֝לִ֗ין עַל־אֲבוּסֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: Is [the] wild ox willing to serve you, or will it spend the night at your manger?
pieces: Will the wild ox agree to serve you? \q Will it stay the night beside your feeding trough?

L.9: Will the wild ox be willing to serve you? \q Or will it spend the night at your manger?

R.9: Will the wild ox agree to work for you? \q Will it stay by your feeding trough at night?

decisions.choice: the wild ox: the aurochs, a great wild bull
decisions.reason: The word (re'em) names a huge, strong wild ox, now extinct, a picture of untamed strength (Numbers 23:22; Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 22:22). The old Greek translation called it "the one-horned", and some later translations followed it with "unicorn"; the Hebrew means a real wild ox with two horns (Deuteronomy 33:17).

decisions.choice: serve you, your manger: the life of the tame ox
decisions.reason: The tame ox works the fields and is fed at its owner's trough (Isaiah 1:3). The wild ox looks like it, but will do neither.

decisions.choice: feeding trough
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use a word most readers know for the place where animals are fed.

records.source: הֲֽתִקְשָׁר־רֵ֭ים בְּתֶ֣לֶם עֲבֹת֑וֹ אִם־יְשַׂדֵּ֖ד עֲמָקִ֣ים אַחֲרֶֽיךָ׃
records.gloss: Will you bind [the] wild ox in [the] furrow [with] its rope, or will it harrow [the] valleys after you?
pieces: Can you tie the wild ox with a rope to plow a furrow? \q Will it follow you and break up the soil in the valleys?

L.10: Can you bind the wild ox in the furrow [with] its rope? \q Or will it harrow the valleys after you?

R.10: Can you tie a rope on the wild ox and make it plow? \q Will it follow you and work your fields in the valleys?

decisions.choice: bind in the furrow with its rope: harness it to plow
decisions.reason: A working ox is tied with ropes and kept in the furrow as it plows. The question asks whether Job can do that with the wild ox.

decisions.choice: harrow: break up the clods after plowing
decisions.reason: The verb means to break up and level the plowed soil (Isaiah 28:24; Hosea 10:11). "After you" pictures the ox following its driver across the field.

decisions.choice: to plow a furrow; break up the soil (B); make it plow, work your fields (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the farming words mean (m1, m2).

records.source: הֲֽתִבְטַח־בּ֭וֹכִּי־רַ֣ב כֹּח֑וֹ וְתַעֲזֹ֖ב אֵלָ֣יו יְגִיעֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: Will you trust in it because great [is] its strength, and will you leave to it your labor?
pieces: Will you rely on it because its strength is great? \q Will you leave your heavy work to it?

L.11: Will you trust in it because its strength [is] great, \q and will you leave your labor to it?

R.11: Will you depend on it because it is so strong? \q Will you let it do your hard work?

decisions.choice: a question expecting "no"
decisions.reason: The wild ox is strong enough for any work, yet that very strength cannot be harnessed. No one could rely on it.

decisions.choice: labor: hard work, or what is gained by it
decisions.reason: The word (yegia') means toil, and also what toil produces (10:3). Here it is the work of the farm.

records.source: הֲתַאֲמִ֣ין בּ֭וֹכִּי־יָשִׁ֣יב זַרְעֶ֑ךָ וְֽגָרְנְךָ֥ יֶאֱסֹֽף׃
records.gloss: Will you trust in it that it will bring back your seed, and [to] your threshing floor gather [it]?
pieces: Can you trust it to bring in your grain \q and gather it to your threshing floor?

L.12: Will you trust in it that it will bring back your seed \q and gather [it to] your threshing floor?

R.12: Can you count on it to bring your harvest home \q and gather it onto your threshing floor?

decisions.choice: bring back, as the Hebrew is read aloud
alternatives: return, as the Hebrew is written
decisions.reason: The consonants as written give "it will return"; the scribes' note for reading aloud gives "it will bring back". The second fits the object, "your seed", and is followed here. The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: seed: the harvested grain
decisions.reason: "Seed" here is the grain of the harvest, brought in from the field.

decisions.choice: gather to your threshing floor
decisions.reason: Harvested grain was carried to the threshing floor, a flat open place where it was threshed and winnowed (Ruth 3:2). Oxen did this work (Deuteronomy 25:4); the wild ox will not.

records.source: כְּנַף־רְנָנִ֥ים נֶעֱלָ֑סָה אִם־אֶ֝בְרָ֗ה חֲסִידָ֥ה וְנֹצָֽה׃
records.gloss: [The] wing of ostriches flaps joyfully; [but is it] a pinion of a stork and plumage?
pieces: The ostrich flaps her wings with joy, \q but are they the wings and feathers of the stork?

L.13: The wing of the ostriches flaps joyfully; \q but [are they] the pinion and plumage of a stork?

R.13: The ostrich happily flaps her wings, \q but her wings are not like the stork's.

decisions.choice: ostriches
decisions.reason: The word (renanim) occurs only here; it seems to come from a root meaning to cry out, from the bird's loud call. The eggs left in the sand (verses 14-15) and the speed that outruns a horse (verse 18) show that the ostrich is meant. Some older translations took it as "peacocks".

decisions.choice: a question: are her wings like the stork's?
alternatives: though her pinions and feathers are like a stork's
decisions.reason: The second line is hard. Read as a question, it contrasts the ostrich's flapping wings, which cannot lift her, with the wings of the stork. The words could also mean that her feathers are fine, like a stork's; or, with a slightly different reading, ask whether her wings are "kindly". Each reading leads into verses 14-16, where the ostrich does not care for her eggs.

decisions.choice: stork: the bird whose name sounds like "kind"
decisions.reason: The Hebrew name of the stork (chasidah) sounds like the word for faithful or kind, from the same root as the word for steadfast love. The stork was known for caring for its young; the ostrich is not (verses 14-16).

decisions.choice: her wings are not like the stork's
alternatives: are they the wings and feathers of the stork?
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into a plain statement of its point (m2), and leaves the feathers out.

records.source: כִּֽי־תַעֲזֹ֣ב לָאָ֣רֶץ בֵּצֶ֑יהָ וְֽעַל־עָפָ֥ר תְּחַמֵּֽם׃
records.gloss: For she leaves to the earth her eggs, and on [the] dust she warms [them].
pieces: She leaves her eggs on the ground \q and lets them warm in the sand.

L.14: For she leaves her eggs to the earth \q and warms [them] on the dust.

R.14: She lays her eggs on the ground \q and lets the warm sand heat them.

decisions.choice: she leaves her eggs on the ground
decisions.reason: The ostrich lays her eggs in a shallow hollow in the sand, open to the sun. The poem pictures her leaving them there, unlike birds that build nests out of reach.

decisions.choice: she warms them: she lets the dust warm them
decisions.reason: The verb says she warms the eggs, but the place named is the dust. The point is that the warm sand, not the mother, keeps them warm.

decisions.choice: lets them warm in the sand (B); lets the warm sand heat them (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say how the eggs are warmed (m2), and say "sand" for the dust of the desert ground.

records.source: וַ֭תִּשְׁכַּח כִּי־רֶ֣גֶל תְּזוּרֶ֑הָ וְחַיַּ֖ת הַשָּׂדֶ֣ה תְּדוּשֶֽׁהָ׃
records.gloss: And she forgets that a foot may crush it, and [the] animal of the field may trample it.
pieces: She forgets that a foot may crush them, \q that a wild animal may trample them.

L.15: And she forgets that a foot may crush it, \q and the animal of the field may trample it.

R.15: She forgets that someone might step on them \q or a wild animal might crush them.

decisions.choice: it: the eggs
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "it", meaning the eggs together, or each egg.

decisions.choice: the animal of the field: any wild animal
decisions.reason: "Animal of the field" means a wild beast, one that lives in the open and is not kept by people.

decisions.choice: someone might step on them
decisions.reason: Readable says who the "foot" belongs to: anyone passing by.

records.source: הִקְשִׁ֣יחַ בָּנֶ֣יהָ לְּלֹא־לָ֑הּ לְרִ֖יק יְגִיעָ֣הּ בְּלִי־פָֽחַד׃
records.gloss: She treats harshly her young as [if they were] not hers; in vain [is] her labor, without fear.
pieces: She treats her young harshly, as if they were not hers; \q she has no fear that her labor may be wasted.

L.16: She deals harshly with her young, as if [they were] not hers; \q her labor [is] in vain, [yet she is] without fear.

R.16: She is hard on her chicks, as if they were not her own. \q She does not care if all her work is wasted.

decisions.choice: she does not fear that her labor will come to nothing
alternatives: though her labor is in vain, she has no fear
decisions.reason: The second line has no verb: "in vain her labor, without fear". It means that she is not troubled that the work of laying her eggs may be lost.

decisions.choice: the ostrich seen as careless of her young
decisions.reason: Israel's poets saw the ostrich as a hard mother: "cruel, like ostriches in the wilderness" (Lamentations 4:3). The poem describes the bird as people saw it, leaving its eggs and running off.

decisions.choice: she has no fear that her labor may be wasted (B); She does not care if all her work is wasted (R)
alternatives: her labor is in vain, without fear
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable join the verbless phrases of the Hebrew into one clause, as m1 reads them.

records.source: כִּֽי־הִשָּׁ֣הּ אֱל֣וֹהַּ חָכְמָ֑ה וְלֹא־חָ֥לַק לָ֝֗הּ בַּבִּינָֽה׃
records.gloss: For God made her forget wisdom, and did not give a share to her in understanding.
pieces: For God has made her forget wisdom \q and has given her no share of understanding.

L.17: For God made her forget wisdom \q and did not give her a share in understanding.

R.17: God did not give her wisdom; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave her no share of good sense.

decisions.choice: God speaks of himself as "God"
decisions.reason: Though God is the speaker, he names himself here in the third person with the word 'Eloah, rendered "God" throughout Job. Speakers in Hebrew poetry often do this (40:9, 19).

decisions.choice: her lack of sense is part of how God made her
decisions.reason: The ostrich's foolish ways are not a mistake in creation; God made her so. Yet he also gave her speed (verse 18). Each creature has what God chose to give it.

decisions.choice: did not give her wisdom; good sense
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that she was not given wisdom, which is what "made her forget" means here, and uses "good sense" for understanding.

records.source: כָּ֭עֵת בַּמָּר֣וֹם תַּמְרִ֑יא תִּֽשְׂחַ֥ק לַ֝סּ֗וּס וּלְרֹֽכְבֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: At [the] time [when] on high she lifts herself, she laughs at the horse and at its rider.
pieces: Yet when she rises up to run, \q she laughs at the horse and its rider.

L.18: When she lifts herself up on high, \q she laughs at the horse and at its rider.

R.18: But when she gets up and runs, \q she laughs at the horse and its rider, because she is faster.

decisions.choice: lifts herself up: rises to run
decisions.reason: The verb is rare and its exact sense is unsure. It seems to mean to rise or rouse herself; some take it as flapping the wings as she runs. Either way the ostrich takes off at speed.

decisions.choice: she laughs at the horse: she can outrun it
decisions.reason: The ostrich cannot fly, but it runs faster than a horse. A bird without sense (verse 17) still scorns the horse and its rider, who cannot catch her.

decisions.choice: because she is faster
decisions.reason: Readable says why she laughs (m2).

records.source: הֲתִתֵּ֣ן לַסּ֣וּס גְּבוּרָ֑ה הֲתַלְבִּ֖ישׁ צַוָּאר֣וֹ רַעְמָֽה׃
records.gloss: Do you give to the horse strength? Do you clothe its neck [with] a mane?
pieces: Do you give the horse its strength? \q Do you clothe its neck with a flowing mane?

L.19: Do you give the horse [its] might? \q Do you clothe its neck with a mane?

R.19: Did you make the horse strong? \q Did you give its neck a mane?

decisions.choice: a mane
decisions.reason: The word occurs only here. It is related to the word for thunder, so some old translations said the horse's neck was clothed "with thunder". It is best taken as the mane that tosses and shakes on the horse's neck.

decisions.choice: strength: might for battle
decisions.reason: The word (gevurah) is used of a warrior's might. The horse described in verses 19-25 is the war horse.

decisions.choice: a flowing mane
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "flowing" to bring out the movement in the word (m1).

records.source: הְֽ֭תַרְעִישֶׁנּוּ כָּאַרְבֶּ֑ה ה֖וֹד נַחְר֣וֹ אֵימָֽה׃
records.gloss: Do you make it leap like the locust? The majesty of its snorting [is] terror.
pieces: Do you make it leap like a locust? \q Its proud snorting strikes terror.

L.20: Do you make it leap like the locust? \q The majesty of its snorting [is] terror.

R.20: Do you make it jump like a grasshopper? \q Its loud snorting makes people afraid.

decisions.choice: make it leap: make it spring and quiver
decisions.reason: The verb means to shake or quake. The war horse bounds forward like a locust; Joel 2:4 makes the same comparison the other way, saying the locusts look like horses.

decisions.choice: the majesty of its snorting: its splendid, frightening snort
decisions.reason: The word (hod) means splendor or majesty. The horse's snort is grand, and it fills the enemy with terror (Jeremiah 8:16).

decisions.choice: grasshopper; makes people afraid
decisions.reason: Readable uses the insect most readers know and says who is frightened.

records.source: יַחְפְּר֣וּ בָ֭עֵמֶק וְיָשִׂ֣ישׂ בְּכֹ֑חַ יֵ֝צֵ֗א לִקְרַאת־נָֽשֶׁק׃
records.gloss: They paw in the valley, and it rejoices in strength; it goes out to meet weapons.
pieces: It paws the ground in the valley and delights in its strength; \q it charges out to meet the weapons.

L.21: They paw in the valley, and it rejoices in [its] strength; \q it goes out to meet [the] weapons.

R.21: It paws at the ground in the valley, glad to be so strong. \q It charges out to face the enemy's weapons.

decisions.choice: they paw: the horses, or its hooves
decisions.reason: The verb is plural, though the horse is singular in the rest of the verse. The plural may mean war horses in general, or the hooves; ancient translations have a singular verb. The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: paw: dig at the ground
decisions.reason: The verb means to dig. The horse scrapes the ground, eager to charge. The same verb is used in verse 29 for the eagle searching out its prey.

decisions.choice: weapons: the armed enemy
decisions.reason: The word means weapons or armor, and stands for the armed troops the horse charges into.

decisions.choice: It paws
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the singular so the verse speaks of one horse throughout (m1).

records.source: יִשְׂחַ֣ק לְ֭פַחַד וְלֹ֣א יֵחָ֑ת וְלֹֽא־יָ֝שׁ֗וּב מִפְּנֵי־חָֽרֶב׃
records.gloss: It laughs at fear and is not dismayed, and does not turn back from before a sword.
pieces: It laughs at fear and is not afraid; \q it does not turn back from the sword.

L.22: It laughs at fear and is not dismayed, \q and it does not turn back from the sword.

R.22: It laughs at fear and is never afraid. \q It does not run away from the sword.

decisions.choice: laughs at fear: scorns what makes others afraid
decisions.reason: As the ostrich laughs at the horse (verse 18) and the wild donkey at the town (verse 7), the war horse laughs at fear. The word for fear is the one used in verse 16 of the ostrich's lack of fear for her young.

decisions.choice: turn back from before a sword: retreat from the fight
decisions.reason: "From before" means from facing it. The horse does not turn away even when swords are drawn against it.

records.source: עָ֭לָיו תִּרְנֶ֣ה אַשְׁפָּ֑ה לַ֖הַב חֲנִ֣ית וְכִידֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: On it rattles a quiver, [the] blade of spear and javelin.
pieces: The quiver rattles at its side, \q along with the flashing spear and javelin.

L.23: On it the quiver rattles, \q the flashing blade of spear and javelin.

R.23: Arrows rattle in the quiver on its side, \q and spears and javelins flash beside it.

decisions.choice: the rider's weapons on the horse
decisions.reason: The quiver of arrows and the spears belong to the rider or charioteer. They rattle and flash as the horse charges.

decisions.choice: blade: the flashing head of the spear
decisions.reason: The word means a flame, and so the shining blade of a weapon (Judges 3:22).

decisions.choice: javelin: a short spear for throwing
decisions.reason: The word (kidon) names a weapon like a javelin (1 Samuel 17:6, 45). Some take it as a curved sword; it is a weapon carried into battle in either case.

decisions.choice: Arrows rattle in the quiver
decisions.reason: Readable says what rattles: the arrows inside the quiver.

records.source: בְּרַ֣עַשׁ וְ֭רֹגֶז יְגַמֶּא־אָ֑רֶץ וְלֹֽא־יַ֝אֲמִ֗ין כִּי־ק֥וֹל שׁוֹפָֽר׃
records.gloss: With shaking and agitation it swallows [the] ground, and it does not stand still when [the] sound of the horn.
pieces: Trembling with excitement, it devours the ground; \q it cannot stand still when the horn sounds.

L.24: With trembling and excitement it swallows the ground, \q and it does not stand still at the sound of the horn.

R.24: It is so excited that it races across the ground. \q It cannot stand still when the trumpet sounds.

decisions.choice: swallows the ground: covers the ground at full speed
decisions.reason: The horse runs so fast that it seems to swallow the ground under it.

decisions.choice: stand still: stand firm, stay in place
decisions.reason: The verb (he'emin) usually means to believe or trust (as in verse 12), and some old translations took it so here: it does not believe it is the horn. Its root sense, to be firm or steady, fits the picture better: the horse cannot keep still.

decisions.choice: the horn: the ram's horn signal for battle
decisions.reason: The shofar, a ram's horn, was blown to call troops to battle (Judges 3:27; 7:18).

decisions.choice: trumpet (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "trumpet" for the ram's horn as a signal, the word most readers know for a call to battle; Literal and Balanced keep "horn".

records.source: בְּדֵ֤י שֹׁפָ֨ר׀יֹ֘אמַ֤ר הֶאָ֗ח וּֽ֭מֵרָחוֹק יָרִ֣יחַ מִלְחָמָ֑ה רַ֥עַם שָׂ֝רִים וּתְרוּעָֽה׃
records.gloss: At every [blast of the] horn it says, Aha! And from afar it smells [the] battle, [the] thunder of [the] commanders and [the] battle cry.
pieces: Whenever the horn blows, it snorts, Aha! \q It smells the battle from far away, \q the thunder of the commanders and the war cry.

L.25: At every [blast of the] horn it says, Aha! \q And from afar it smells the battle, \q the thunder of the commanders and the war cry.

R.25: When the trumpet sounds, it snorts, Aha! \q It smells the battle from far away. \q It hears the commanders shouting and the battle cry.

decisions.choice: at every blast: as often as the horn sounds
decisions.reason: The phrase means "as often as" or "whenever": each time the horn blows.

decisions.choice: Aha!: a cry of eager delight
decisions.reason: The word is a cry of glee (Psalm 35:21). The horse's snort is pictured as a shout of joy at the coming fight.

decisions.choice: smells the battle from afar: senses it before it comes
decisions.reason: The horse picks up the battle while it is still far off, as an animal catches a scent.

decisions.choice: the thunder of the commanders: their loud shouted orders
decisions.reason: The commanders' voices boom like thunder over the field, joined by the soldiers' war cry.

decisions.choice: it snorts
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say how a horse "says" Aha (m2).

decisions.choice: It hears the commanders shouting
decisions.reason: Readable adds "hears" and turns the thunder into shouting (m4).

records.source: הֲֽ֭מִבִּינָ֣תְךָ יַֽאֲבֶר־נֵ֑ץ יִפְרֹ֖שׂ כְּנָפָ֣יו לְתֵימָֽן׃
records.gloss: ? By your understanding does [the] hawk soar, spread its wings toward [the] south?
pieces: Is it by your understanding that the hawk takes flight \q and spreads its wings toward the south?

L.26: Is it by your understanding that the hawk soars \q [and] spreads its wings toward the south?

R.26: Did you teach the hawk to fly \q and spread its wings to go south?

decisions.choice: the hawk soars: the falcon or hawk takes flight
decisions.reason: The bird (nets) is a hawk or falcon. The verb, found only here, seems to mean to fly up or soar, from the word for a wing feather.

decisions.choice: toward the south: the yearly migration
decisions.reason: Hawks fly south over the land of Israel each autumn. Who taught them when and where to go? Jeremiah 8:7 also speaks of birds that know their seasons.

decisions.choice: Did you teach the hawk
decisions.reason: Readable puts the question in plain terms: was it Job's knowledge that showed the hawk how to fly?

records.source: אִם־עַל־פִּ֭יךָ יַגְבִּ֣יהַּ נָ֑שֶׁר וְ֝כִ֗י יָרִ֥ים קִנּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Or at your mouth does [the] eagle mount up, and that it makes its nest high?
pieces: Is it at your command that the eagle flies high \q and builds its nest up on the heights?

L.27: Or is it at your command that the eagle mounts up \q and makes its nest on high?

R.27: Does the eagle fly high because you tell it to? \q Did you tell it to build its nest so high?

decisions.choice: at your mouth: at your command
decisions.reason: "At the mouth of" means at someone's word or order (Numbers 9:18, "at the mouth of the LORD").

decisions.choice: eagle: the great bird of prey, eagle or vulture
decisions.reason: The word (nesher) covers the eagle and the griffon vulture. Verse 30, where it gathers where the dead are, fits the vulture well; "eagle" is kept as the common name of the great bird of the heights.

records.source: סֶ֣לַע יִ֭שְׁכֹּן וְיִתְלֹנָ֑ן עַֽל־שֶׁן־סֶ֝֗לַע וּמְצוּדָֽה׃
records.gloss: [On the] rock it dwells and spends the night, on [the] tooth of [the] rock and [the] stronghold.
pieces: It lives on the cliffs and stays there at night, \q on a rocky crag, its fortress.

L.28: It dwells on the rock and spends the night \q on the tooth of the rock and [its] stronghold.

R.28: It lives on the cliffs and sleeps there at night, \q safe on a high, rocky point.

decisions.choice: the tooth of the rock: a jagged crag
decisions.reason: A "tooth" of rock is a sharp, pointed crag (1 Samuel 14:4-5).

decisions.choice: stronghold: a safe high place
decisions.reason: The word means a fortress. The eagle's cliff is its fortress, where no enemy can reach it.

decisions.choice: a rocky crag, its fortress (B); safe on a high, rocky point (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable explain the picture of the "tooth" (m1); Readable says "safe" for what the stronghold gives (m2).

records.source: מִשָּׁ֥ם חָֽפַר־אֹ֑כֶל לְ֝מֵרָח֗וֹק עֵינָ֥יו יַבִּֽיטוּ׃
records.gloss: From there it spies out food; from afar its eyes look.
pieces: From there it searches for its prey; \q its eyes see it from far away.

L.29: From there it spies out food; \q its eyes look from afar.

R.29: From there it looks for food. \q Its sharp eyes can see a long way.

decisions.choice: spies out: searches for
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to dig (verse 21, of the horse pawing the ground); here, as in the spies of Joshua 2:2-3, it means to search out.

decisions.choice: food: the prey it hunts
decisions.reason: Its food is the animals it hunts, as verse 30 shows.

decisions.choice: sharp eyes
decisions.reason: Readable adds "sharp" to bring out the point of seeing from far away.

records.source: וְאֶפְרֹחָ֥יו יְעַלְעוּ־דָ֑ם וּבַאֲשֶׁ֥ר חֲ֝לָלִ֗ים שָׁ֣ם הֽוּא׃פ
records.gloss: And its young ones gulp blood, and where [the] slain [are], there [is] it.
pieces: Its young ones gulp down blood, \q and where the dead bodies are, there it is.

L.30: And its young ones gulp blood; \q and where the slain are, there it is.

R.30: Its chicks drink blood. \q Wherever there are dead bodies, the eagle is there.

decisions.choice: gulp: drink greedily
decisions.reason: The verb occurs only here. It seems to mean to gulp or suck down.

decisions.choice: where the slain are, there it is
decisions.reason: Jesus uses a saying like this one: "Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather" (Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37).

decisions.choice: God provides even for the birds of prey
decisions.reason: The survey of wild animals ends as it began in 38:39-41, with food for young ones. God feeds even the fierce birds, in ways Job neither sees nor controls. God's first speech ends here; 40:1-2 is its closing challenge.

decisions.choice: the eagle
decisions.reason: Readable names the bird for clarity, at the end of a long passage about many animals.
